content: 1. HIV Treatment Coverage: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends treatment for all people living with HIV to achieve viral suppression. This indicator is critical for monitoring national health strategies, program management, and donor programming. It also aligns with the second 95 target, which aims for 95% of individuals aware of their HIV-positive status to access ART by 2025. 2. Numerator and Denominator for ART Coverage: The numerator is the number of people on ART at the end of the reporting period, derived from HIV patient monitoring data (e.g., ART registers, patient records, or electronic medical records). For key populations, survey data may be required. The denominator for ART coverage is the estimated number of people living with HIV, obtained from epidemiological models like Spectrum AIM. To assess progress toward the second 95 target, the denominator includes the number of people living with HIV who know their status. 3. Retention and Attrition Analysis: Retention and attrition analyses are essential for understanding ART program outcomes. The numerator excludes individuals who stopped treatment, died, or were lost to follow-up during the reporting period. These categories should be reported separately to calculate the number of people on ART. 4. Viral Load Suppression (VLS): VLS is a key clinical outcome and reflects adherence to ART. It is also central to achieving the third 95 target. The numerator includes individuals on ART for at least six months with at least one routine viral load test showing suppression during the reporting period. The denominator includes all individuals on ART for at least six months with a routine viral load result. 5. Early Viral Load Testing: WHO recommends routine viral load testing at six months after ART initiation to assess suppression and identify individuals needing adherence support. The time window for early viral load monitoring includes a margin of ±1 month (i.e., testing can occur between five and seven months after ART initiation). 6. Late ART Initiation: Late initiation is a risk factor for treatment failure and is important to monitor. The numerator includes individuals with a baseline CD4 count <200 cells/mm³ at ART initiation, while the denominator includes all individuals initiating ART during the reporting period with a baseline CD4 count. 7. Follow-Up for Non-Suppressed Viral Load: It assesses the quality of follow-up care for individuals with non-suppressed viral loads. The numerator includes individuals who received a follow-up test within three months, and the denominator includes all individuals with a viral load ≥1000 copies/mL during the reporting period. 8. ART Toxicity: ARV-related toxicities are a common reason for treatment discontinuation or drug substitution. The numerator includes patients who stopped treatment or switched regimens due to toxicity, while the denominator includes all ART patients during the reporting period. 9. HIV-Exposed Infants: Early Infant Diagnosis (EID): The percentage of HIV-exposed infants receiving a virological test within two months (and 12 months) of birth. Early testing supports timely ART initiation for HIV-positive infants and counseling for prevention in those with negative results. ARV Prophylaxis Coverage: The percentage of HIV-exposed infants started on ARV prophylaxis at birth. This is critical for reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission in the immediate postpartum period. ART Coverage for Pregnant Women: The percentage of HIV-positive pregnant women who received ART during pregnancy and/or at labor and delivery. This is essential for preventing vertical transmission and achieving the Treat All strategy. 10. Viral Suppression in Pregnant Women: The numerator includes women on ART during pregnancy who delivered at a facility and were virally suppressed at delivery. The denominator can be program-based (women on ART delivering at a facility) or population-based (all estimated HIV-positive pregnant women). 11. Key Populations and ART Access: It is central to improving access to treatment and care services among key populations, such as men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. These indicators collectively provide a comprehensive framework for monitoring and improving HIV care and treatment outcomes, aligning with global targets to end the HIV epidemic.
